episode_title: Remembering Paulien Cornelisse, plus MPs push back on taxing small savers
description: The Netherlands is mourning writer and comedian Paulien Cornelisse, who died at 50 while she was still on TV every night. We also cover the end of the border checks and the wider powers that replace them, MPs pushing back on taxing small savers, mortgage rates at their highest this year, and tougher sentences for attacks on public workers. Plus a Van Gogh that could set an auction record, what the Fabel Friet queue may be doing to house prices next door, and what's on in Amsterdam this weekend.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Netherlands is mourning Paulien Cornelisse. The writer and comedian died of cancer at 50, and she was still on television every single night.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In The Hague, MPs are pushing back on a plan that would make hundreds of thousands of small savers pay tax on their savings.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Plus, the border checks are over, but the border police are getting new powers. It's Thursday, the first of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We start with a loss a lot of people here are feeling this morning. Paulien Cornelisse died on Wednesday at the Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, the cancer hospital in Amsterdam. She was 50, and her loved ones were with her.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: If you're new here, you might not know the name. But there's a good chance you've seen her face. She was a writer and a cabaretier. That's a Dutch comedian who does one-person theatre shows, closer to stand-up theatre than song and dance. Really, though, she was a kind of national language-watcher.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Her breakthrough was a 2009 book called 'Taal is zeg maar echt mijn ding.'

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Which roughly means 'Language is, like, totally my thing.' And the title is the joke. She picked apart everyday Dutch: filler words, office jargon, all the little things people say without really meaning them. It sold seven hundred thousand copies.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Which is enormous for a country this size.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It really is. She also wrote these wonderfully absurd books about a guinea pig who works in an office. De verwarde cavia, 'The Confused Guinea Pig.' One of them won a big readers' award last year. Also last year, she wrote the Boekenweekessay, the essay commissioned every year for national Book Week. It sold out on the second day, which had never happened before.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: For a lot of people, she was simply part of the evening. Since September last year she'd been the one-person jury on De Slimste Mens, 'The Smartest Person.' It's a nightly quiz and one of the most-watched shows in the country. She did it alongside presenter Herman van der Zandt.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Those episodes were recorded before the summer. She was diagnosed in 2024 and was still having chemo this year. So in every episode she wore a hat or a cap. The chemo had made her hair fall out, and she didn't want a wig.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: After talking with her family, the broadcaster KRO-NCRV dropped Wednesday's episode. The rest are moving back a day, and new dates will be announced. She was also due back on stage at the end of October, with a new show at the DeLaMar theatre in Amsterdam. It was called 'Waar was ik gebleven,' 'Where was I.' That's been cancelled, and ticket holders will get refunds.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Tributes came in all day. Prime Minister Rob Jetten called her 'sharp, funny and incredibly kind.' Herman van der Zandt said she was 'sweet, funny and, even between treatments, wonderfully energetic.'

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Her last weekly column in de Volkskrant came out just a week ago. In it she was puzzling over the word 'apegapen.'

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It's a Dutch expression for being utterly exhausted. She was still curious about words right to the end.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There's no word yet on a public farewell. Paulien Cornelisse lived in Amsterdam with her partner, Chris Bajema, and their sons.

segments.title: Border checks end, wider spot checks begin

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now to the rest of the day's news, starting at the border. If you've driven to Belgium or Germany in the last couple of years, you may have slowed down for a checkpoint. As of today, those checkpoints are gone.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Remind me who brought those in?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Marjolein Faber, the asylum minister in the previous cabinet, which was led by Geert Wilders' PVV. They started in December 2024, were meant to last six months, and kept getting extended. They ended yesterday.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The checks are run by the Koninklijke Marechaussee, the Royal Military Police. It's a police force that's part of the military. It guards the borders, Schiphol and the royal family. Think border protection crossed with military police. And normally, inside the Schengen area, there are no passport checks between countries at all. Countries can only bring them back temporarily, and they have to justify it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But this isn't the end of checks. The Marechaussee is going back to its regular spot checks, called Mobiel Toezicht Veiligheid, or Mobile Security Monitoring. They can happen anywhere within twenty kilometres of the Belgian and German borders, at changing times and places, based on intelligence and risk. And they now have more room than before.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How much more?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They can now check on the same road for up to 120 hours a month instead of 90, and the six-hour daily limit is gone. They can still only stop part of the traffic. But if a train is selected, every passenger on it can be checked, and the same goes for a selected flight from another Schengen country. No more than a quarter of the trains or flights on a route can be picked.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the Marechaussee is pleased. Their line is that smugglers can't count on a checkpoint packing up after six hours anymore.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The cabinet, now led by Rob Jetten of the centrist D66, says it wants to keep fighting illegal migration and people smuggling. It's also responding to complaints from border towns, businesses and residents about the traffic chaos.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Did the old checks actually work?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Between December 2024 and March this year, about six hundred foreigners were refused entry, mostly for lacking valid papers. Two hundred and seventy people were arrested for things like document fraud and smuggling. Asylum seekers can't be turned away at the border. And last year the national audit office found the checks didn't reduce migration, though they could help against illegal migration.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: One practical note: Germany is keeping its own border checks until at least March 2027. So if you're heading east, you may still hit a checkpoint. It'll just be a German one.

segments.title: MPs balk at taxing small savers

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: To The Hague. Earlier this week we told you the cabinet wants to cut the tax-free return in box 3, the tax on savings and investments, from 1,800 euros to 1,000. That would pull about 850,000 more people into paying it. Yesterday, MPs pushed back hard.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: This was day one of the Algemene Financiële Beschouwingen, parliament's big annual budget debate. Remember, the coalition of D66, VVD and CDA has no majority in either house. It needs opposition votes for every budget.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And on this one, it isn't getting them. JA21, ChristenUnie and the SGP oppose the plan, and Pro is against it on principle. So a majority looks out of reach. SGP MP Flach called it 'a fine on thrift or successful entrepreneurship.'

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So does the coalition back down?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's bending. After a barrage of questions, all three coalition parties said they'd look at alternatives. CDA MP Van Dijk called the plan 'an unfortunate point.' But D66's Oosterhuis set a condition: any alternative has to raise the same money from taxing wealth. That's 473 million euros.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Has anyone found 473 million euros lying around?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not yet. Pro suggested taxing larger fortunes instead, but there's no concrete alternative on the table. Most parties did welcome the bigger change, which is taxing gains only when you sell. That starts in 2028 for shares, bonds and second homes, and in 2030 for crypto.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the opposition was angrier about income tax.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Both income tax bands go up next year. That's only partly offset by a bigger labour tax credit, worth at most 173 euros. The Council of State, the government's top legal adviser, had already pointed out that almost all of next year's six billion in extra taxes falls on workers.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: BBB MP Vermeer called it 'taking 200 euros, giving back 100 and expecting you to be happy.'

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: JA21 and Pro say they'll only back the cabinet if that increase is scaled back. There was also friction over the backup plan to cut education. D66 blamed that on an 'overzealous civil servant,' but the VVD confirmed it's the agreed fallback if the social security savings fall short. On top of all this, the cabinet wants to nearly halve the tax-free allowance on savings in 2027, to about 31,000 euros per person. That's not law yet. Finance Minister Heinen responds today.

segments.title: Mortgage rates climb, estate agents face a register

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Staying with money. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level this year. The average ten-year fixed rate with NHG is now four and a half percent. A few weeks ago it was around four point one.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: NHG is the Nationale Hypotheekgarantie, a government-backed guarantee for homes below a set price. It gets you a lower rate. And before you ask, this isn't the European Central Bank. The ECB has kept its rate steady. It's the capital markets, where banks raise money, with worries about inflation, energy and geopolitics.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And it bites quickly here, because Dutch rules tie how much you can borrow to the interest rate. Take a couple earning 90,000 euros a year. At three and a half percent they could borrow about 413,000 euros. At four and a half, it's about 395,000. And the monthly payment rises by roughly 200 euros per percentage point on a 350,000-euro loan.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So do prices fall?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not for now. Demand still far outstrips supply. But Amsterdam is cooling. In the second quarter, prices there were less than one percent higher than a year earlier. Nationally they were up more than four percent. ABN Amro expects that cooling to spread across the country.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Then there's the people selling you the house.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Housing Minister Boekholt-O'Sullivan is taking oversight of estate agents, or makelaars, away from the industry itself. Every agent will have to be on a government register to work. There'll be a complaints desk, and a disputes committee that can strike agents off. Agents will also have to show buyers the biedlogboek, the log of every bid made on a home.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Which matters if you've ever bought here. You bid blind, often way over asking. And right now you don't even need a government licence to be an agent. Her research found almost a third of people had at least one bad experience with an agent, but only two percent filed a complaint. Concrete proposals are due early next year.

segments.title: Jail as the starting point for attacks on public workers

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From today, attacking someone doing a public job brings a much tougher response from prosecutors. The Openbaar Ministerie, the national prosecution service, says every case now goes to court. No more settling with a fine or community service. Prosecutors must ask for double the usual sentence, with prison as the starting point.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Who counts as a public worker?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's a broad group: police, emergency workers, transport staff, referees, teachers, judges, politicians and journalists, among others. Justice Minister David van Weel gave an example. A first offender tries to seriously assault an emergency worker, with no weapon and no injury. In principle, prosecutors would ask for three months in prison. If the victim were an ordinary member of the public, it'd be eighty hours of community service. Judges keep their discretion. The change follows pressure from MPs after New Year's Eve, when police and firefighters were attacked.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: On the same day, the rail union VVMC sent what's called a brandbrief, literally a 'fire letter.' It's an urgent open letter to politicians.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: NS, the national railway, has logged more than five thousand reports of aggression against staff so far this year. That's almost double all of 2023. Conductors were knocked unconscious at Rotterdam Blaak and Den Dolder. At Almere Centrum, an employee was badly bitten on the thumb.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The union wants more security staff on trains. It also wants back the enforcement powers senior conductors lost in 2022, when NS dropped them to save money. NS says it shares the concerns. It's giving every conductor a body camera, testing batons for security staff and hiring more people.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In Amsterdam, a trial treating crack addiction with medicine has been halted. The drug is dexamphetamine, which is normally prescribed for ADHD.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The idea is a bit like methadone for heroin: you give a controlled stimulant to cut the cravings. A project called REDUCE spent twelve years developing a long-acting version, with the city health service, the GGD, as a partner.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But the IGJ, the national health inspectorate, has stopped production at a hospital it won't name. It says it's 'concerned about the quality of the medicine,' and that its investigation started before the trial did. It hasn't said what the concerns are. The first participants had already started taking it, and their treatment has been interrupted. Alderman Alexander Scholtes couldn't say how many people are affected.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the city's not happy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Scholtes said 'the only promising method' for heavily addicted people is now off the table. He and Mayor Femke Halsema asked Health Minister Sophie Hermans to bring everyone together before November first. Hermans said she understands their concerns, but the inspectorate is independent and 'I have confidence in their judgment.' She didn't commit to a meeting. The GGD estimates there are three to nine thousand crack users in the city.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: One more from The Hague. The Netherlands is threatening to hold back money from Italy unless it starts taking back asylum seekers.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Under EU rules, the country where an asylum seeker first enters is usually responsible for them. Many people arrive in Italy and then travel north, and for years Italy has mostly refused to take them back.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In June, asylum minister Bart van den Brink signed a declaration in Rome saying returns would resume. In practice, little has happened. Dutch courts keep blocking transfers, most recently in three cases last week, because the minister hadn't shown Italy has reception places ready. Under the new EU Migration Pact, the Netherlands chose to pay into a support fund for Mediterranean countries rather than take in asylum seekers. Its share this year is about eleven million euros. Yesterday Van den Brink told MPs: 'If something doesn't work, we won't pay.'

segments.title: A Van Gogh that could set a record

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Okay, some lighter stuff. Sam, have you got a spare 180 million dollars?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Let me check. Nope, I've got a tram card and half a stroopwafel.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then you'll miss out. On November 18th, Sotheby's in New York is auctioning Van Gogh's 'Chestnut Trees in Blossom.' It's expected to go for around 180 million dollars, maybe 200 million or more.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The current Van Gogh auction record is 117 million, so this would blow right past it. And hardly anyone has seen it in public for sixty years. The last time was at the Guggenheim in 1964. An Argentine couple, the Blaquiers, bought it in 1975 and kept it in their private collection in South America. Now their children are selling.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He painted it in May 1890, days after he arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise outside Paris. He died there two months later. And one of its early owners was his brother, Theo.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: From Theo's family to a 200-million-dollar bidding war. There's a whole story in that.

segments.title: Fabel Friet and the price of a queue

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And our closer. Earlier this week we told you about neighbours of Fabel Friet, the TikTok-famous chip shop in the Nine Streets, taking the city to court over the queues. Now somebody's put a number on it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Rosa van der Drift, a PhD candidate at TU Delft, published a study in the journal Regional Studies. She looked at more than six thousand Amsterdam home sales and found homes within 500 metres of the shop sold for almost five percent less than similar homes further away. That's about 41,000 euros.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Within seventy metres, the gap was more than eleven percent.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Forty-one thousand euros. That's a lot of fries.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There's a big caveat, though. The study covers 2015 to 2023, but the queues only started when the shop went viral in 2022. And the study doesn't pin down the cause.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Could be the crowds, the noise, the litter, or the queue itself. Quick language tip for newcomers: whether you say friet or patat depends on which part of the country you're in. So choose carefully.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The judge is expected to rule in a few weeks. Meanwhile, an opinion piece in Het Parool told the complainers they're 'warmly welcome in Purmerend,' a commuter town north of Amsterdam.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Ouch. It's the classic reply to people in the centre: if you live there, you get the crowds.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And if you'd rather queue for something free this weekend…

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: …how about a thousand free oysters? On Saturday from four to nine, IJver on the NDSM Wharf in Noord is celebrating seven and a half years, and the wharf itself turns 132. There'll be a thousand free bitterballen too, beer and spritz for two-fifty, and a DJ. Entry's free and there's no sign-up, but the food only lasts while supplies do.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So get there early. If you want something grander, Joe Hisaishi, the composer behind the Studio Ghibli films, is conducting the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra at the Ziggo Dome in Zuidoost, Friday through Sunday. He'll play piano too. There's music from Spirited Away, Ponyo and Howl's Moving Castle, with film clips on a giant screen.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It's the orchestra's first time in the city's biggest concert hall. One tip, though: the run also includes a Beethoven's Ninth night, so check the date before you book. Unless you really like surprises.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Starting tonight there's the Afrovibes Festival, now in its 23rd year. It's dance, theatre, music and spoken word by artists from Africa and the diaspora, and this year's theme is land, ancestry and belonging. It's at De Brakke Grond, the Flemish cultural centre in the city centre, from a quarter past seven tonight, then Friday and Saturday evenings. Over the weekend it's also at Framer Framed and the Bijlmer Parktheater, though the Bijlmer dates may still change.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: For art lovers, Chez Matisse opens Saturday at the H'ART Museum in the Plantage. It has more than eighty works, including La Blouse roumaine. It runs until mid-February, so there's no rush if opening weekend's too busy.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And on Sunday there's the Sunday Market at Westergas in Westerpark: street food, local makers and art. You can make an afternoon of it with a walk in the park.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's it for today. Thanks for listening to Dutch Daily Briefing. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. Look after each other, and we'll see you tomorrow.
